title: At the Gate: Boaz Redeems, and a Son Is Born
summary: Boaz goes to the town gate, gathers ten elders, and offers the nearer relative the right to redeem Elimelech's land. When he learns that taking the land also means marrying Ruth and raising an heir for the dead man, the relative steps aside and seals it with his sandal. Boaz marries Ruth, the LORD gives them a son, Obed, and the women of Bethlehem celebrate with Naomi. The book closes with a short genealogy from Perez to David.
story: Chapter 3 ended with Naomi telling Ruth to wait, confident that Boaz would not rest until the matter was settled that day. Chapter 4 shows him doing exactly that. The book opened with three funerals, a famine, and a woman who said the LORD had brought her back empty; it closes with a wedding, a birth, and Naomi holding a grandson. The private kindness of the harvest field and the threshing floor now becomes public and legal, witnessed by the whole town. And the last lines reach beyond the family to the nation: the child is the grandfather of David. The small story of two widows turns out to be the prelude to Israel's kingship, which is why Christian Bibles place Ruth directly before 1 Samuel.
historical:
The events are set in the time of the judges, before Israel had kings, but the narrator writes for readers who needed an explanation of the sandal custom because it belonged to former times in Israel (verse 7). That remark and the closing genealogy, which ends with David, show that the book was written at least in the time of the monarchy. Whether it comes from the reign of David or Solomon, from later in the monarchy, or from the period after the exile is debated, as the introduction to Ruth explains.

The genealogy has a parallel in 1 Chronicles 2:9-15, and several of its names appear elsewhere. Perez was the son of Judah by Tamar (Genesis 38), and Nahshon was the leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness (Numbers 1:7). The list moves quickly from the patriarchal period to David with only ten names, which suggests that, like many ancient genealogies, it selects key figures rather than recording every generation.
cultural:
The gate of an ancient town was more than an entrance. It was a covered complex with benches or chambers where elders sat, business was done, and legal disputes were heard; it functioned as the town's courthouse and public square. By sitting at the gate and summoning ten elders, Boaz convenes a formal legal session, and the whole transaction is done before witnesses so that no one can later contest it.

The legal logic is compressed. Naomi has a right to family land that belonged to Elimelech, and the nearest redeemer has the first right and duty to buy it so it stays in the family (Leviticus 25:25). At first the relative agrees, since adding a field to his holdings is attractive. But Boaz adds that the purchase comes with Ruth, and that any son she bears will carry the dead man's name and inherit the land. The relative would pay for a field that would pass to another man's line and weaken his own estate. So he gives up his right. The sandal ceremony, in which the relative removes his sandal and hands it to Boaz, served as a public sign that a right had been transferred, perhaps because setting foot on land was a way of claiming it. Deuteronomy 25:9 describes a related but harsher ceremony when a brother refuses levirate duty, and Ruth 4 differs from it in important ways, which is one reason scholars debate how the customs of redemption and levirate marriage fit together in this story.
literary: The chapter has two halves: a legal scene at the gate (verses 1-12) and a family scene around the child (verses 13-17), followed by a genealogy (verses 18-22). The nearer relative is never named; Boaz calls him by a Hebrew phrase something like so-and-so, perhaps a deliberate touch, since the man who would not preserve another's name loses his own in the story. Boaz, by contrast, acts so that the name of the dead will not disappear, and the elders pray that his name will be famous in Bethlehem. The women's chorus, which in chapter 1 asked whether this could be Naomi, returns to bless the LORD for giving her a redeemer. Their praise of Ruth as “better to you than seven sons” (verse 15) is extraordinary in a culture that prized sons. The genealogy lists ten generations from Perez to David and places Boaz in the seventh position, a pattern many readers think is intentional.

outline.t: Boaz convenes the elders at the gate
Boaz buys the land and takes Ruth; the town blesses the marriage
Obed is born, and Naomi's emptiness is filled
The line from Perez to David

doctrines.note: The LORD is said to act directly only twice in the book: he gives food to his people (1:6) and gives Ruth conception (4:13). Everything else happens through human choices. The genealogy then shows where these ordinary events were leading, to Israel's greatest king, so the book teaches that God works purposefully through hidden, everyday faithfulness.

A Moabite woman, from a people Israel regarded with suspicion, becomes the great-grandmother of David. The book quietly insists that loyalty to Israel's God, not ethnic origin, makes a person part of his people, anticipating the inclusion of the nations in Christ.

The legal scene shows covenant law working as intended: land stays in families, the vulnerable are protected, and the dead are not forgotten. Boaz goes beyond the minimum the law required, which is the book's picture of covenant faithfulness.

words.note: Qanah, to buy or acquire. It is the verb of the property transaction, and the text uses it both for the field and, uncomfortably for modern readers, for taking Ruth as wife. In verse 5 the written Hebrew text and the traditional reading differ on whether the verb means you acquire or I acquire, which affects how the exchange is understood. The verb belongs to legal language rather than implying that Ruth was property.

Shem, name. It appears seven times in the chapter. To raise up the name of the dead meant to keep a man's family line and claim on the land alive through an heir. The chapter plays on the word: the dead man's name is preserved, Boaz's name is to be famous, the unnamed relative stays nameless, and the child is named by the women of the town.

Nachalah, inheritance, the family's allotted share of the land. In Israel's theology the land belonged to the LORD and each family held its portion as a trust from him, which is why keeping it within the family mattered so much. The redeemer's fear of damaging his own inheritance is what makes him withdraw.

Ed, witness. Boaz twice tells the elders and people that they are witnesses, and they reply that they are. Public witness made the agreement binding in an oral culture, as a signed document would today.

christ: The chapter's final word is David, and through David the book points toward the Messiah. Matthew's genealogy of Jesus follows this list (Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David) and pointedly includes Ruth by name, alongside Tamar, who is also mentioned in verse 12 (Matthew 1:3-6). Jesus is thus descended from a line that includes foreigners and people who came in by grace rather than birthright. Boaz's role also offers a pattern: a redeemer who takes on a cost at his own expense so that a family's name and inheritance are restored. The New Testament speaks of Christ redeeming his people and securing for them an inheritance (Ephesians 1:7, 14). That connection is thematic rather than predictive; Ruth does not foretell Jesus, but it helps supply the language of kinsman, redemption, and inheritance in which the gospel is later told.

hard.q: Deuteronomy 23:3 says no Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD. How can a Moabite woman become an ancestor of David?
hard.a: The tension is real, and the book seems aware of it, since it calls Ruth the Moabitess again and again. Several answers have been given. Later rabbinic tradition held that the prohibition applied to Moabite men and not to women, so Ruth's marriage was lawful. Others note that Ruth has explicitly taken Israel's God as her own (1:16), and argue that the law excluded Moab as a hostile people, not individual foreigners who joined Israel in faith. Many modern scholars read the book as deliberately testing a strict application of the law, holding up a Moabite whose faithfulness puts many Israelites to shame. These views are not exclusive. What is clear is that the book presents Ruth's inclusion as a blessing from the LORD and makes her the mother of Israel's royal line.

questions: The unnamed relative protected his own inheritance and lost his place in the story. When has protecting yourself kept you from an act of generosity?
The women of Bethlehem say Ruth is better to Naomi than seven sons. What does that suggest about how God values loyalty and love over status?
The book ends with a genealogy that turns a family story into part of Israel's history. How might your ordinary faithfulness belong to a larger story you cannot yet see?
